analysis.one_liner: Requires new televisions to have built-in circuitry that displays closed captions.
analysis.headline: The House passed the bill by voice vote on October 1, 1990, and its identical Senate companion, S. 1974, went on to become the Television Decoder Circuitry Act of 1990.
analysis.plain_summary: The bill requires that any television with a screen of 13 inches or more, whether made in the U.S. or imported, include built-in decoder circuitry that displays closed captions — so deaf and hard-of-hearing viewers no longer have to buy and hook up a separate TeleCaption decoder box. The FCC must write performance and display standards within 180 days of enactment, and after five years must revisit the rules so caption decoding keeps working as TV technology changes. The requirement takes effect in October 1992, giving manufacturers lead time.
analysis.who_benefits: The roughly 24 million deaf and hard-of-hearing Americans, who gain direct access to captioned TV without buying a separate decoder; the nearly 38% of older Americans with some hearing loss; hearing and hearing-impaired children and adults building reading skills; and immigrants learning English. Captioning services and broadcasters also gain a much larger potential captioned audience, which the bill's findings say creates an incentive to caption more programming.

how_it_helps.text: Builds caption decoding into every new TV with a screen of 13 inches or more sold in the U.S., eliminating the need for consumers to buy a separate TeleCaption decoder and connect it to their set.

Opens television access to the more than 24 million Americans who are deaf or hearing-impaired, plus the nearly 38% of older Americans with some hearing loss, letting captions appear automatically on any new set.
Serves people beyond the deaf community: the findings note captions help hearing and hearing-impaired children with reading, improve adult literacy, and help immigrants learning English.
Grows the captioned audience enough, in Congress's judgment, to give broadcasters an incentive to caption more programming, multiplying the benefit over time.
Directs the FCC to write performance standards within 180 days and, five years later, to update the rules so decoder circuitry keeps serving caption users as broadcast technology evolves.

analysis.who_pays: Television manufacturers — domestic and foreign alike — must build decoder circuitry into every set of 13 inches or larger shipped, made, or imported for U.S. sale. Congress's own findings describe the added cost as nominal, and it would mostly surface as a small increase in TV prices for all buyers, including people who never use captions. The FCC bears the cost of writing and later updating the standards.
analysis.who_pays_short: TV makers, via small per-set costs

drawbacks.text: The mandate adds a per-set cost to every television of 13 inches or larger, which lands partly on all TV buyers — including the many who never turn captions on. Congress itself characterized the added cost as 'nominal' and built in more than two years of lead time before the October 1992 effective date, but it is a genuine cross-subsidy from all set buyers to caption users.

The rules pin caption display to 1980s-era technical specifications (a 1980 PBS engineering report and a 1985 decoder specification) on line 21 of the broadcast signal. The bill only requires the FCC to review compatibility after five years, so standards could lag behind new broadcast technologies until then.
Sets with screens smaller than 13 inches are exempt, so owners of small portable TVs still need a separate decoder box to see captions.

analysis.benefit_vs_cost: The cost side is small and well-contained: a nominal per-set component cost, spread across every TV sold, with a long lead time and a built-in five-year technology review. The benefit side is large — television access for more than 24 million deaf and hard-of-hearing Americans, plus literacy and language-learning spillovers. This is a well-designed mandate with a strongly favorable cost-benefit balance.

outcome.mechanism: The House passed its version by voice vote on October 1, 1990, then set it aside so the identical Senate companion, S. 1974, could carry the measure the rest of the way — that Senate bill became the Television Decoder Circuitry Act of 1990, signed into law on October 15, 1990 as Public Law 101-431.

narrative.text: Rep. Major Owens of New York introduced the bill on March 14, 1990 with a bipartisan group of original cosponsors including Reps. Markey, Gunderson, Bonior, Berman, Lloyd, Slattery, Synar, Wyden, Bilirakis, Chandler, Madigan, and Oxley.

The bill went to the Energy and Commerce Committee and its Telecommunications and Finance Subcommittee, which amended and forwarded it in July 1990; the full committee amended it again and reported it on September 27, 1990 (H. Rept. 101-767), placing it on the Union Calendar.
On October 1, 1990, Rep. Markey moved to suspend the rules and pass the bill — a fast-track procedure allowing limited debate — and the House agreed by voice vote, with no recorded opposition.

Rather than work out differences between the House and Senate versions, the House laid its bill on the table and directed further action to the identical Senate companion, S. 1974; that Senate bill became the Television Decoder Circuitry Act of 1990 (Public Law 101-431), signed October 15, 1990.

outcome.who_came_out_ahead: Deaf and hard-of-hearing Americans — along with older viewers, children building literacy, and English learners — came out ahead: within two years, closed-caption decoding was built into every new TV of 13 inches or larger sold in the United States.

for.name: Rep. Major Owens
for.what_they_did: Introduced the Television Decoder Circuitry Act on March 14, 1990, marshaling 12 original cosponsors from both parties.

for.name: Rep. Edward Markey
for.role: Original cosponsor; senior Energy and Commerce member on telecommunications
for.what_they_did: Cosponsored the bill at introduction and, on October 1, 1990, moved to suspend the rules and pass it, bringing it to the House floor for a voice vote.

for.name: House Energy and Commerce Committee
for.what_they_did: Amended the bill in the Telecommunications and Finance Subcommittee and in full committee, then reported it on September 27, 1990 (H. Rept. 101-767) and placed it on the Union Calendar.

sides.party_line_note: The 41 cosponsors split 31 Democrats and 10 Republicans, the bill cleared committee on a voice vote, and the House passed it by voice vote with no recorded opposition on either side.

industries.note: The bill forces every set of 13 inches or larger sold in the U.S. to include caption decoder circuitry, adding a per-set cost Congress itself called nominal, phased in by October 1992. The industry's interest in avoiding the mandate ran against the accessibility benefit it delivered, though no opposition appears in the record.

With decoding built into every new set, the potential captioned audience grows enormously, which the bill's findings say gives broadcasters an incentive to caption more programming. The National Captioning Institute's technical specifications became the legal standard the FCC must enforce.
